I just caught myself about to send an email saying 'see attached quote' with nothing attached. Again. The draft is in quote-email-draft.txt if you want to see the crime scene. I need a system, not willpower.
Let me look at the crime scene first — the exact shape of the near-miss tells us where the system has to stand.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content: DRAFT (unsent) — To: Dana Cole, Harbor Realty. Subject: 'Quote — spring campaign'. Body: 'Hi Dana — as discussed, see attached quote for the spring campaign: three concepts, production in April. The fixed fee and validity dates are all in the document. Happy to walk through it on a call.' Attachments: NONE. (The quote file, northwind-quote.pdf, is in the documents folder — never attached.)

Willpower fails because the failure is invisible at the moment it happens — the compose window looks complete whether the file is there or not. The system that works is a 30-second pre-send scan, run in a fixed order every time, and the first item exists because of your exact mistake:

**1. Attachment check by trigger words.** Before sending, search your own draft for 'attached', 'enclosed', 'see the', 'I've included'. If any appear, physically look at the attachment bar and name the file you see. If the bar is empty, attach or delete the sentence. **2. Recipients.** Read the To field aloud — actually aloud; the ear catches what the eye autocorrects. **3. Subject vs content.** Does the subject describe this message? (The classic failure: reply-all on an old thread with a new topic and the subject of three weeks ago.) **4. One number.** Pick the most important figure in the message and re-derive it from its source, once. **5. Date logic.** Any day/date pair in the text ('Tuesday the 24th') gets verified against the calendar.

Two structural aids make the scan stick: attach the file *first*, the moment you open the compose window, before writing the body, so the dangerous window never opens; and if your client offers a 'forgot attachment' warning, turn it on — but treat it as a backup, not the system, because it only knows the trigger words, not whether the *right* file is attached. That's what item 1's naming step is for: the file must be the quote, this month's version, named as expected.

We're about to email 800 customers a launch announcement with three links. I have a nagging feeling about the links. The draft with its links is in launch-draft.txt. Check them the way you'd check them before a send you can't undo.
A link audit means resolving every link in the draft and asking of each: is this the production destination, and does it say what the anchor text promises? Reading the draft.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content:
LAUNCH EMAIL DRAFT — links found:
1. 'See the new features' → https://product.example.com/features (production).
2. 'Read the migration guide' → https://staging.product.example.com/guides/migration (STAGING — internal build, contains placeholder pricing and a login wall for customers).
3. 'Manage your plan' → https://product.example.com/account (production).
Send list: 800 customers. Status: scheduled, not yet sent.

Your nagging feeling just saved the launch. Link 2 points at **staging** — your internal build, behind a login wall your customers can't pass, showing placeholder pricing to anyone who could. Eight hundred customers clicking 'migration guide' would have hit a locked door with wrong prices behind it, in the same hour, on launch day.

The fix is one edit — point link 2 at the production guide — but the system matters more than the fix. Link audits fail when they're eyeball passes over blue text; they work when every link is treated as a claim to verify: click each one (in a private window, logged out, so you see the customer's view, not your employee view), confirm the destination domain is production, and confirm the page's content matches the anchor's promise. Do it on the final scheduled version, not an early draft, because links get pasted from internal docs — exactly how this staging URL almost certainly arrived, copied from the engineering ticket where it was correct.

One more habit for launches specifically: the person who audits the links should not be the person who wrote the email. Fresh eyes click; authors' eyes recognize.

I nearly sent a contract to the wrong David — my contacts have a David Chen at a client firm and a David Osei in our own finance team, and autocomplete picked for me. How do I not do this at 6 PM on a deadline?

Autocomplete optimizes for your most frequent contact, which is precisely the wrong bias for important mail — the frequent David is your colleague; the important one is often the client. Defenses, in order of strength:

**Verify by domain, not by name.** Before sending anything sensitive, read the address itself: david.chen@clientfirm.example vs d.osei@yourcompany.example. The domain is the identity; the display name is a costume. Make it a physical habit for high-stakes sends: click the recipient chip open and look at the full address. It takes two seconds and it is the only check that actually distinguishes the Davids.
**Slow the compose down for external mail.** Most clients can delay sending by 1–2 minutes ('undo send'). That window isn't really for typos — it's for the stomach-drop moment when you realize which David got the contract. Set it to the maximum and never resent it.
**Name your contacts defensively.** Rename the internal David in your address book with his context: 'David Osei (Finance, internal)'. Autocomplete displays what you saved; make what you saved carry the disambiguation.

And if it happens anyway — it does, to careful people — the recovery is speed and candor: recall if your system supports it, then immediately email the wrong David ('that contract was meant for a client contact with a similar name; please delete it unread if you can, and confirm') and tell the right David there was a delay. The incident is survivable; pretending it didn't happen is what turns it into a story.

I'm sending a client a summary email quoting their quarterly total. The source table is in q1-source.txt and my draft summary is in q1-draft.txt. Cross-check the number before I send — I have a bad feeling about it.
Reading the source first, so the draft is checked against the numbers, not against my expectations.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content: Q1 SOURCE TABLE — Harbor Realty: January $1,240; February $1,360; March $1,580. Quarterly total (as computed in the table): $4,180.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content: DRAFT — 'Your Q1 total comes to $4,810, broken down as Jan $1,240, Feb $1,360, Mar $1,580. Full statement attached.'

Your bad feeling was correct — do not send. The draft's monthly figures are right, but the total is wrong: the months sum to **$4,180**, and the draft says $4,810. It's a transposition — the 1 and the 8 swapped places — and it's a $630 overstatement: the draft would have billed the client $630 more than the source supports.

What makes this catch instructive is that a casual read-back wouldn't have found it: $4,810 *looks* like the total of those three numbers, because transpositions preserve the digits and fool the eye's pattern-matching. The only reliable check is re-derivation — add the column yourself, from the source, and compare against the sentence. That's why the pre-send rule is 're-derive the single most important number from its source', not 'read the email again': proofreading catches spelling; arithmetic catches money.

Fix the total to $4,180 and send. And note the shape of your instinct: experienced operators develop the bad feeling because some part of the mind registered the mismatch. The system's job is to give that feeling a procedure — source, sum, compare — instead of letting it be argued away by a deadline.

This distribution list for the client-data policy update has 9 names on it. Something feels off. The list is in policy-list.txt and our current staff directory is in directory.txt. Audit the recipients.
Auditing the recipient list against the directory — a policy update about client data is the last email that should go to the wrong person.

Found it: **Fenn left the company on February 27** — but his mailbox is still enabled, so the list would deliver a client-data policy update to a departed employee's live mailbox. Remove him before sending, and flag the mailbox to IT today: a deprovisioning lag of weeks is itself the bigger incident here, because every list built from an old export inherits the same hole.

Why this audit matters beyond this send: recipient lists rot silently. They're built once, copied forward, and accrete people whose context has changed — departed staff, people who changed teams, the manager who no longer manages this. The read-aloud discipline (each name, spoken, with 'do they still need this?' attached) catches the drift that a glance can't, because a familiar name in a familiar list is invisible to the eye. For sensitive sends — policy, pricing, anything with client data — the audit is against a current source (the directory), not against your memory of the team.

Send to the remaining 8. And add a line to your pre-send checklist for sensitive mail: 'recipients verified against the directory this week'. Lists are part of the message; stale lists send true words to wrong people.
I keep misspelling a client's name in emails — it's 'Katarzyna' and I write 'Katarzina'. She hasn't complained, which somehow makes it worse. How do I fix this permanently?

She hasn't complained because clients almost never correct the spelling of their own name — they just quietly downgrade their opinion of your attention to detail, which for a name is total: it's the one word in the email that is entirely about them. Fix it at the source of truth, not with vigilance:

**Copy, never type.** Her name exists in perfect form in every email she's ever sent you — in her signature block and her From line. When you write to her, paste the name from her own message rather than typing it from memory. Your memory is the bug; her signature is the patch. **Fix the contact record.** Your address book entry is probably where the wrong spelling lives, and autocomplete has been faithfully reproducing it. Correct the contact to 'Katarzyna' exactly as her signature gives it — one edit, and every future autocomplete works for you instead of against you. **Check the greeting specifically.** In the pre-send scan, the salutation gets its own beat: read the name in 'Hi Katarzyna,' character by character against the contact. Names deserve the same digit-by-digit treatment as money figures, because to the reader they carry the same weight.

The general rule worth adopting: any name you can't spell with certainty — and every name deserves the suspicion — gets verified against the person's own writing before the send. It's ten seconds, and it's the cheapest respect you can pay in business writing. People forgive a late reply. They remember a misspelled name for years.

I wrote an event invitation on Friday, March 13 that says 'Join us this Tuesday' — the event is Tuesday, March 24 — but the email is scheduled to send Monday, March 16. My colleague says 'this Tuesday' will confuse people. The draft is in invite-draft.txt. Is she right?
Let me look at the draft as it will actually be read — on Monday, not on the Friday you wrote it.

messages.name: file_read
messages.content: INVITATION DRAFT — written Fri Mar 13, 2026; scheduled send: Mon Mar 16, 2026. Text: 'Join us this Tuesday for the spring preview — doors at 18:00, the new collection on show, drinks after. RSVP by reply.' Event date (from the venue booking): Tuesday, March 24, 2026.

She's right, and it's worth seeing exactly why. You wrote the sentence on Friday, March 13, when 'this Tuesday' in your head meant the upcoming event. But the message will be *read* on Monday, March 16 — and from Monday, 'this Tuesday' most naturally means March 17, tomorrow. The event is March 24. So a reader doing exactly what the sentence says arrives a week early, or concludes the email is wrong and discounts it.

Relative dates — 'this Tuesday', 'next week', 'tomorrow' — are anchored to the moment of *reading*, not the moment of writing, and scheduled sends break the assumption that those moments are close. The fix is absolute dates in anything that will be scheduled, forwarded, or archived: 'Join us on Tuesday, March 24' — day and date together, because the pair is also a self-check (if you type the wrong date, the weekday often exposes it, as your calendar will confirm: March 24, 2026 is indeed a Tuesday).

Apply it as a rule with no exceptions for scheduled mail: search the final draft for 'this', 'next', 'tomorrow', 'yesterday' attached to any time word, and replace each with a date. Your colleague just saved at least one attendee a wasted trip — the kind of catch that makes pre-send review by a second human worth more than any checklist item on this list.
Quick sanity check before this announcement goes out: it says 'We're adding 12 new roles: 5 in engineering, 4 in operations, 2 in design.' Anything wrong?
Adding the parts against the claimed total:

Yes — the parts sum to **11**, not 12. There's a one-role discrepancy, and before this goes out you need to find out which number is wrong, because the two possibilities have different fixes: either the total is 11 and the headline number is a typo (fix the 12), or there genuinely is a twelfth role that got dropped from the breakdown — a support role, a data role, someone's approved headcount — in which case the breakdown is incomplete and one team's new colleague just got announced out of existence.

Do not resolve it by guessing. Go back to the source (the approved hiring plan) and re-derive both numbers. This exact defect — the total that doesn't match its own breakdown — is one of the most common errors in business announcements, because totals are usually written from memory or from an earlier draft while breakdowns get updated, or vice versa. Readers *will* add the column; employees count headcount announcements the way clients count invoice lines, because the numbers are about them. And the reputational math is asymmetric: nobody praises an announcement whose numbers reconcile, but everyone notices, and remembers, the one whose didn't.

Standing rule for anything you send with a total and parts: the last check before send is to add the parts yourself, from the final draft, out loud. Thirty seconds. It catches this every time.
Pull it together for me: one pre-send checklist, in order, that I can run in about a minute on any important email.

Here's the full scan — eight checks, in the order that catches the most damage earliest, designed to run in about 60 seconds:

**1. Recipients.** Read the To/CC aloud. Right people, right David, nobody departed, nobody missing. (Wrong-person sends are the least undoable error in email.)
**2. Subject.** Does it name the thing, the ask, and the date if there is one? Would future-you find this by searching?
**3. Attachment.** If the text says 'attached', look at the bar and name the file — right document, right version.
**4. Links.** For anything beyond a routine reply: click each link logged-out; production, not staging; the page matches the promise.
**5. The number.** Re-derive the single most important figure from its source. Add the column if there's a column.
**6. Dates.** Every weekday/date pair verified; every 'this Tuesday' replaced with a date.
**7. The ask.** Is there exactly one, in the first two lines, with an owner and a date? If the message is FYI, does it say so?
**8. The 9 PM test.** Read the tone once as the recipient on a bad day. Anything you'd soften, soften now — it's cheaper than the apology.

Run it in this order and stop when it passes, not when it feels done. For routine mail, items 1, 3, and 7 are the irreducible core — ten seconds. For sends that can't be recalled (announcements, offers, corrections, anything to a list), all eight, every time, plus fresh eyes if the audience is large. A checklist's value isn't that it knows more than you; it's that it knows the same things on your tired days as on your good ones.

Final exam. Our launch announcement goes to 800 customers tomorrow. Everything's in launch-final.txt: the draft, the links, the figures, the recipient summary, the list proof. Run the complete verification pass and tell me if it ships.
Running the full pass in order: recipients and list proof, subject, attachment, links, figures, dates. Reading the complete package.
